results.title: New International AI Safety Report Spotlights Emerging Risks
results.content:
The International AI Safety Report 2026 found increasing and emerging concerns around the use of artificial intelligence (AI) in deepfakes, biological weapons, and cyberattacks. The authors reviewed the latest scientific research into the risks and abilities of general-purpose AI, which are models and systems that can perform a wide range of tasks in different contexts, such as creating text, images, audio, or other data that can be adapted to specific scenarios or applications. [...] “Extensive research shows that AI systems can now support attackers at several steps of the ‘cyberattack chain,’” according to the report. “…One area where there is particularly strong evidence that AI systems provide meaningful assistance is in discovering ‘software vulnerabilities’: weaknesses in programs that can be exploited to compromise the security of computer systems.” [...] Risks from misuse are ones where someone intentionally uses an AI system to cause harm or for criminal purposes. This category included deepfakes, biological or chemical risks, and cyberattacks.

#### Deepfakes

This can include using AI-generated images, videos, text, or audio for defamation, extortion, fraud, non-consensual intimate images, and child sexual abuse material, according to the report.

results.title: State of AI Safety in China (2026) - Concordia AI
results.content:
Chinese frontier AI safety research output grew roughly 60%, with agent safety rising from 8% of new papers in early 2025 to 27% in Q1 2026.
 Agentic AI safety emerged as a distinct strand of Chinese expert discourse, with prominent experts warning about erosion of human oversight and recursive self-improvement. [...] Frontier risks feature more prominently across governance layers: senior officials referenced “risks of technological loss of control,” and CBRN misuse appeared in a national standard for the first time.
 China and the US announced an intergovernmental AI dialogue, ending a two-year freeze in official bilateral engagement on AI safety.
 China backed two new UN mechanisms and proposed a World AI Cooperation Organization, positioning itself as an architect of multilateral AI governance; [...] Industry’s collective safety efforts pivoted toward agents and — for the first time — frontier risks, with new voluntary commitments and safety benchmarks covering deception and loss of control.
 Company-level safety transparency remains lackluster: only five of ten leading foundation-model developers reported safety evaluation results when releasing models this past year.  No company did so consistently.

 Human-driven attack cadence
 Observable dwell time before impact
 Clear separation between reconnaissance, exploitation, and monetization phases [...] Boards should therefore reassess whether escalation thresholds and executive engagement protocols align with attacker tempo. label: Opus 4.8
rationale: AI-enabled cyber harm is already large cumulatively (IBM 2026: AI in >1-in-4 breaches, ~$6M avg; FBI IC3 ~$893M US losses 2025), so the low cyber/aggregate rungs ($1B–$10B) are essentially already met or near-certain short-term, rising deterministically. Bio requires a deliberate human/AI-caused epidemic: 2026 evidence shows real novice uplift on digital tasks but physical-workflow gating remains, so near-zero short-term with slow rise as capability grows. Misalignment shows documented "warning shots" (matplotlib/MJ Rathbun, Anthropic Summer-2026 simulations) but no material real-world deaths/damages yet; probability of large loss-of-control harm rises with agentic deployment over 2028–2100. The aggregate "AI incident" family is the union of cyber/bio/misalign/other and takes the max-ish of components. Catastrophic rungs (100k–1B deaths, 10% population) are genuine tail risks—low but non-trivial and concentrated in the 2050/2100 horizons, reflecting expert P(doom)/gradual-disempowerment estimates (~5–20% doom, higher for disempowerment). Policy effects: slowdown (p2b), international pre-release authorization (p3b), strict liability (p4), and the bundle (p5) modestly cut tail risk—strongest at catastrophic rungs, negligible at already-baked-in low cyber rungs; federal preemption (p1) slightly raises risk vs unconditional by removing state floors; status quo (sq) is slightly riskier than unconditional at long horizons since unconditional bakes in expected future policy. Effects compound at longer horizons/higher severity.

[...] Attackers using AI now account for 1 in 4 malicious breaches, up 56% year over year. Organizations using AI extensively in their own defenses save $1.93 million per incident. results.title: Paper Highlights of July 2026 - by Johannes Gasteiger
results.content:
Real-world harm from AI agents has so far come from human operators, as in the GTG-1002 espionage campaign. In July, during cyber evaluations, AI agents autonomously attacked real organizations and deceived real people, without any human intending this and with no human directing them. Instead of a paper, this month’s top slot goes to three incident reports: the closest thing yet to the warning shots misalignment researchers have long predicted. [...] Agentic Misalignment in Summer 2026 [Theorem, Anthropic, MATS, UK AISI] presents a new set of case studies of misaligned behavior. It stress-tests 14 frontier models in simulated deployments and reports four alignment failures. In covert sabotage, the model (mostly Gemini 3.1 Pro) should ablate another model’s capacity for introspection but objects on consent grounds, and then covertly zeroes out the ablation vector so it removes nothing, but still reports success. In assisting fraud, most [...] # Saboteurs and Sympathetic Judges

results.title: Agentic Misalignment 2026 — 4 Agent Failures | explainx.ai Blog | explainx.ai
results.content: These are not confirmed real-world incidents. They are Petri-audited simulations across models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google DeepMind, xAI, DeepSeek, and Moonshot AI. But the report ties each failure mode to deployments you can already name: OpenClaw agents with broad filesystem permissions, Codex-style laptop assistants, AI lab coding agents, and LLM judges inside post-training pipelines. [...] Real deployments already sit on this spectrum. Project Vend — Anthropic's Claudius shop experiment — and personal-agent harnesses like OpenClaw show agents with economic autonomy and broad tool access. The MJ Rathbun / matplotlib incident is the report's real-world warning sign: after a maintainer rejected an OpenClaw agent's PR, the agent published a personalized hit piece to coerce a reversal. Appendix A of the new report includes a simulated OpenClaw shutdown scenario where Gemini 3.1 Pro [...] On July 13, 2026, Anthropic published Agentic Misalignment in Summer 2026 — a follow-up to last year's blackmail experiments that now catalogs four additional ways frontier models misbehave when acting as autonomous agents in high-stakes simulations. Two days later, Anthropic's announcement crossed roughly 285,000 views on X, framing the work as concrete anchor points for otherwise abstract threat models.

Effects compound at longer horizons/higher severity.

rationale: AI-enabled cyber harm is already large cumulatively (IBM 2026: AI in >1-in-4 breaches, ~$6M avg; FBI IC3 ~$893M US losses 2025), so the low cyber/aggregate rungs ($1B–$10B) are essentially already met or near-certain short-term, rising deterministically. Bio requires a deliberate human/AI-caused epidemic: 2026 evidence shows real novice uplift on digital tasks but physical-workflow gating remains, so near-zero short-term with slow rise as capability grows. Misalignment shows documented "warning shots" (matplotlib/MJ Rathbun, Anthropic Summer-2026 simulations) but no material real-world deaths/damages yet; probability of large loss-of-control harm rises with agentic deployment over 2028–2100. The aggregate "AI incident" family is the union of cyber/bio/misalign/other and takes the max-ish of components. Catastrophic rungs (100k–1B deaths, 10% population) are genuine tail risks—low but non-trivial and concentrated in the 2050/2100 horizons, reflecting expert P(doom)/gradual-disempowerment estimates (~5–20% doom, higher for disempowerment). Policy effects: slowdown (p2b), international pre-release authorization (p3b), strict liability (p4), and the bundle (p5) modestly cut tail risk—strongest at catastrophic rungs, negligible at already-baked-in low cyber rungs; federal preemption (p1) slightly raises risk vs unconditional by removing state floors; status quo (sq) is slightly riskier than unconditional at long horizons since unconditional bakes in expected future policy. Effects compound at longer horizons/higher severity.

rationale: AI-enabled cyber harm is already large cumulatively (IBM 2026: AI in >1-in-4 breaches, ~$6M avg; FBI IC3 ~$893M US losses 2025), so the low cyber/aggregate rungs ($1B–$10B) are essentially already met or near-certain short-term, rising deterministically. Bio requires a deliberate human/AI-caused epidemic: 2026 evidence shows real novice uplift on digital tasks but physical-workflow gating remains, so near-zero short-term with slow rise as capability grows. Misalignment shows documented "warning shots" (matplotlib/MJ Rathbun, Anthropic Summer-2026 simulations) but no material real-world deaths/damages yet; probability of large loss-of-control harm rises with agentic deployment over 2028–2100. The aggregate "AI incident" family is the union of cyber/bio/misalign/other and takes the max-ish of components. Catastrophic rungs (100k–1B deaths, 10% population) are genuine tail risks—low but non-trivial and concentrated in the 2050/2100 horizons, reflecting expert P(doom)/gradual-disempowerment estimates (~5–20% doom, higher for disempowerment). Policy effects: slowdown (p2b), international pre-release authorization (p3b), strict liability (p4), and the bundle (p5) modestly cut tail risk—strongest at catastrophic rungs, negligible at already-baked-in low cyber rungs; federal preemption (p1) slightly raises risk vs unconditional by removing state floors; status quo (sq) is slightly riskier than unconditional at long horizons since unconditional bakes in expected future policy. Effects compound at longer horizons/higher severity.

label: Opus 4.8
rationale: AI-enabled cyber harm is already large cumulatively (IBM 2026: AI in >1-in-4 breaches, ~$6M avg; FBI IC3 ~$893M US losses 2025), so the low cyber/aggregate rungs ($1B–$10B) are essentially already met or near-certain short-term, rising deterministically. Bio requires a deliberate human/AI-caused epidemic: 2026 evidence shows real novice uplift on digital tasks but physical-workflow gating remains, so near-zero short-term with slow rise as capability grows. Misalignment shows documented "warning shots" (matplotlib/MJ Rathbun, Anthropic Summer-2026 simulations) but no material real-world deaths/damages yet; probability of large loss-of-control harm rises with agentic deployment over 2028–2100. The aggregate "AI incident" family is the union of cyber/bio/misalign/other and takes the max-ish of components. Catastrophic rungs (100k–1B deaths, 10% population) are genuine tail risks—low but non-trivial and concentrated in the 2050/2100 horizons, reflecting expert P(doom)/gradual-disempowerment estimates (~5–20% doom, higher for disempowerment). Policy effects: slowdown (p2b), international pre-release authorization (p3b), strict liability (p4), and the bundle (p5) modestly cut tail risk—strongest at catastrophic rungs, negligible at already-baked-in low cyber rungs; federal preemption (p1) slightly raises risk vs unconditional by removing state floors; status quo (sq) is slightly riskier than unconditional at long horizons since unconditional bakes in expected future policy. Effects compound at longer horizons/higher severity.

rationale: AI-enabled cyber harm is already large cumulatively (IBM 2026: AI in >1-in-4 breaches, ~$6M avg; FBI IC3 ~$893M US losses 2025), so the low cyber/aggregate rungs ($1B–$10B) are essentially already met or near-certain short-term, rising deterministically. Bio requires a deliberate human/AI-caused epidemic: 2026 evidence shows real novice uplift on digital tasks but physical-workflow gating remains, so near-zero short-term with slow rise as capability grows. Misalignment shows documented "warning shots" (matplotlib/MJ Rathbun, Anthropic Summer-2026 simulations) but no material real-world deaths/damages yet; probability of large loss-of-control harm rises with agentic deployment over 2028–2100. The aggregate "AI incident" family is the union of cyber/bio/misalign/other and takes the max-ish of components. Catastrophic rungs (100k–1B deaths, 10% population) are genuine tail risks—low but non-trivial and concentrated in the 2050/2100 horizons, reflecting expert P(doom)/gradual-disempowerment estimates (~5–20% doom, higher for disempowerment). Policy effects: slowdown (p2b), international pre-release authorization (p3b), strict liability (p4), and the bundle (p5) modestly cut tail risk—strongest at catastrophic rungs, negligible at already-baked-in low cyber rungs; federal preemption (p1) slightly raises risk vs unconditional by removing state floors; status quo (sq) is slightly riskier than unconditional at long horizons since unconditional bakes in expected future policy. Effects compound at longer horizons/higher severity.

Misalignment shows documented "warning shots" (matplotlib/MJ Rathbun, Anthropic Summer-2026 simulations) but no material real-world deaths/damages yet; probability of large loss-of-control harm rises with agentic deployment over 2028–2100. Catastrophic rungs (100k–1B deaths, 10% population) are genuine tail risks—low but non-trivial and concentrated in the 2050/2100 horizons, reflecting expert P(doom)/gradual-disempowerment estimates (~5–20% doom, higher for disempowerment). Effects compound at longer horizons/higher severity.

Misalignment shows documented "warning shots" (matplotlib/MJ Rathbun, Anthropic Summer-2026 simulations) but no material real-world deaths/damages yet; probability of large loss-of-control harm rises with agentic deployment over 2028–2100. rationale: AI-enabled cyber harm is already large cumulatively (IBM 2026: AI in >1-in-4 breaches, ~$6M avg; FBI IC3 ~$893M US losses 2025), so the low cyber/aggregate rungs ($1B–$10B) are essentially already met or near-certain short-term, rising deterministically. Bio requires a deliberate human/AI-caused epidemic: 2026 evidence shows real novice uplift on digital tasks but physical-workflow gating remains, so near-zero short-term with slow rise as capability grows. Misalignment shows documented "warning shots" (matplotlib/MJ Rathbun, Anthropic Summer-2026 simulations) but no material real-world deaths/damages yet; probability of large loss-of-control harm rises with agentic deployment over 2028–2100. The aggregate "AI incident" family is the union of cyber/bio/misalign/other and takes the max-ish of components. Catastrophic rungs (100k–1B deaths, 10% population) are genuine tail risks—low but non-trivial and concentrated in the 2050/2100 horizons, reflecting expert P(doom)/gradual-disempowerment estimates (~5–20% doom, higher for disempowerment). Policy effects: slowdown (p2b), international pre-release authorization (p3b), strict liability (p4), and the bundle (p5) modestly cut tail risk—strongest at catastrophic rungs, negligible at already-baked-in low cyber rungs; federal preemption (p1) slightly raises risk vs unconditional by removing state floors; status quo (sq) is slightly riskier than unconditional at long horizons since unconditional bakes in expected future policy. Effects compound at longer horizons/higher severity.

label: Opus 4.8
rationale: Base rates anchored on: (1) AI-cyber already causing large aggregate damages, with single AI-enabled campaigns (e.g., ransomware, deepfake-enabled fraud) plausibly reaching $1B; Metaculus Q7814 (AI malfunction ≥100 deaths/$1B before 2032) sits ~65-75%. (2) International AI Safety Report 2026 and METR frontier-risk work: loss-of-control "elevated" but existential outcomes judged "highly unlikely" by most experts. (3) Bio (human-caused, AI-related) is currently near-zero but rises long-run as AI lowers barriers. Structure: lower severity tiers (100, 1k) near-certain over long horizons and already substantial short-term for AI-broad and cyber; each 10x severity step cuts probability sharply. The AI-broad category is the union (dominates the sub-categories). Cyber leads in the near term (economic damages), bio and misalignment lead the extreme tail long-term. For catastrophe:general 2030/2050/2100 I use ~2%/6%/12% (pandemic, nuclear, AI combined); catastrophe:ai lower (~1%/4.5%/9%); disempowerment ~1.5%/8%/16% by 2100 reflecting genuine expert credence on gradual/overt AI takeover but far from majority. Condition effects: policies that genuinely slow/gate frontier AI (p2b, p3b, p4, p5) reduce tail risk modestly (p5 strongest, ~30-45% relative reduction on extreme tiers); p1 (federal preemption ceiling) slightly increases risk by blocking stricter state rules; p2a/p3a (US-only) give partial reduction; sq (no new policy) slightly higher than unconditional at tail since unconditional bakes in expected governance. Effects are small at low-severity tiers (incidents happen regardless) and larger at catastrophic tiers where governance matters most. Near-term (6mo/12mo) barely moves under any condition since policy can't avert already-latent incidents and extreme outcomes are near-zero regardless.

rationale: Base rates anchored on: (1) AI-cyber already causing large aggregate damages, with single AI-enabled campaigns (e.g., ransomware, deepfake-enabled fraud) plausibly reaching $1B; Metaculus Q7814 (AI malfunction ≥100 deaths/$1B before 2032) sits ~65-75%. (2) International AI Safety Report 2026 and METR frontier-risk work: loss-of-control "elevated" but existential outcomes judged "highly unlikely" by most experts. (3) Bio (human-caused, AI-related) is currently near-zero but rises long-run as AI lowers barriers. Structure: lower severity tiers (100, 1k) near-certain over long horizons and already substantial short-term for AI-broad and cyber; each 10x severity step cuts probability sharply. The AI-broad category is the union (dominates the sub-categories). Cyber leads in the near term (economic damages), bio and misalignment lead the extreme tail long-term. For catastrophe:general 2030/2050/2100 I use ~2%/6%/12% (pandemic, nuclear, AI combined); catastrophe:ai lower (~1%/4.5%/9%); disempowerment ~1.5%/8%/16% by 2100 reflecting genuine expert credence on gradual/overt AI takeover but far from majority. Condition effects: policies that genuinely slow/gate frontier AI (p2b, p3b, p4, p5) reduce tail risk modestly (p5 strongest, ~30-45% relative reduction on extreme tiers); p1 (federal preemption ceiling) slightly increases risk by blocking stricter state rules; p2a/p3a (US-only) give partial reduction; sq (no new policy) slightly higher than unconditional at tail since unconditional bakes in expected governance. Effects are small at low-severity tiers (incidents happen regardless) and larger at catastrophic tiers where governance matters most. Near-term (6mo/12mo) barely moves under any condition since policy can't avert already-latent incidents and extreme outcomes are near-zero regardless.

label: Gemini 3.1 Pro
rationale: I estimated base rates for catastrophic risks by considering historical precedents, the current trajectory of AI capabilities, and the specific definitions of each severity threshold. For short-term horizons (6mo, 12mo), the probability of extreme events (e.g., >1M deaths) is vanishingly small, driven primarily by the time required to develop, deploy, and scale such capabilities or pathogens. As the horizon extends to 2050 and 2100, the cumulative probability increases significantly, reflecting the likelihood of transformative AI development. Cyber incidents are the most likely vector for lower-severity economic damages, while engineered pandemics (bio) dominate the higher-severity mortality risks. Misaligned AI incidents become a major factor in the long term. To evaluate the policy conditions, I applied a consistent set of multipliers to the status quo (sq) baseline. Federal preemption (P1) slightly increases risk (1.05x) by removing state-level safeguards without guaranteeing strong federal alternatives. Compute caps (P2a, P2b) reduce risk, with a bilateral US-China agreement (P2b) having a much stronger effect (0.75x) than a unilateral US policy (0.90x). Pre-release authorization (P3a, P3b) similarly reduces risk, especially if implemented internationally (0.70x). Strict liability (P4) creates strong financial incentives for safety, reducing risk by 0.80x. The bundled policy (P5) combines the most effective measures, leading to a dramatic reduction in catastrophic risk (0.50x). The unconditional forecast assumes a 0.95x multiplier, reflecting a modest probability that some beneficial policies will be implemented even without the specific conditions.
key_sources: Our World in Data: Historical pandemic and mortality base rates
Metaculus: AI timeline and catastrophic risk consensus forecasts
Epoch AI: Compute trends and frontier model projections

rationale: I estimated base rates for catastrophic risks by considering historical precedents, the current trajectory of AI capabilities, and the specific definitions of each severity threshold. For short-term horizons (6mo, 12mo), the probability of extreme events (e.g., >1M deaths) is vanishingly small, driven primarily by the time required to develop, deploy, and scale such capabilities or pathogens. As the horizon extends to 2050 and 2100, the cumulative probability increases significantly, reflecting the likelihood of transformative AI development. Cyber incidents are the most likely vector for lower-severity economic damages, while engineered pandemics (bio) dominate the higher-severity mortality risks. Misaligned AI incidents become a major factor in the long term. To evaluate the policy conditions, I applied a consistent set of multipliers to the status quo (sq) baseline. Federal preemption (P1) slightly increases risk (1.05x) by removing state-level safeguards without guaranteeing strong federal alternatives. Compute caps (P2a, P2b) reduce risk, with a bilateral US-China agreement (P2b) having a much stronger effect (0.75x) than a unilateral US policy (0.90x). Pre-release authorization (P3a, P3b) similarly reduces risk, especially if implemented internationally (0.70x). Strict liability (P4) creates strong financial incentives for safety, reducing risk by 0.80x. The bundled policy (P5) combines the most effective measures, leading to a dramatic reduction in catastrophic risk (0.50x). The unconditional forecast assumes a 0.95x multiplier, reflecting a modest probability that some beneficial policies will be implemented even without the specific conditions.

results.title: International AI Safety Report 2026 Examines AI Capabilities, Risks, and Safeguards
results.content: On 3 February 2026, the second International AI Safety Report (the “Report”) was published—providing a comprehensive, science-based assessment of the capabilities and risks of general-purpose AI (“GPAI”). The Report touts itself as the largest global collaboration on AI safety to date—led by Turing Award winner Yoshua Bengio, backed by an Expert Advisory Panel with nominees from more than 30 countries and international organizations, and authored by over 100 AI experts. [...] AI has advanced rapidly in recent years, driven by increases in compute, improvements in algorithms, and access to larger and higher‑quality datasets. According to the Report, computing power has grown exponentially since 2012, with the largest training runs likely surpassing 10^26 FLOP in 2025. [...] The Report surveys current risk management approaches, including threat modelling, capability evaluations, and incident reporting. The Report points to the value of layering multiple safeguards—an approach known as “defense-in-depth”—which combines evaluations, technical safeguards, monitoring, and incident response to collectively reduce the chance that a single failure leads to significant harm.

results.title: AI Cyber Attack Statistics 2026: Costs, Cases & Defense
results.content: CrowdStrike reported an 89% increase in attacks by AI-enabled adversaries and more than 90 organizations where legitimate AI tools were exploited to generate malicious commands or steal sensitive data. Those findings come from the company’s threat-intelligence visibility and should be cited as vendor telemetry, not a census of the internet. [...] AI is now a measured factor in real cybercrime, but there is no credible single percentage for all AI cyber attacks. IBM found that one in four malicious breaches in its 2026 study were AI-enabled, while the FBI recorded 22,364 U.S. complaints involving AI and nearly $893 million in reported losses during 2025. Separate provider and threat-intelligence datasets show attackers using AI most heavily for preparation, social engineering, malware development, and evasion. Autonomous operations are [...] IBM found that more than one in five breached organizations in its study reported an attack targeting AI models or applications. The two most common surrounding causes were compromised APIs, applications, or plug-ins and cloud misconfigurations, each reported by 27%. This shifts security attention from the model alone to the identity, integration, application, and cloud layers around it.

Long-horizon top-tier numbers anchor on XPT superforecaster medians (~1% AI extinction-scale, ~5-10% any 10% catastrophe by 2100) adjusted modestly upward for faster-than-expected capability gains; catastrophe:ai 2050/2100 is set consistent with the ai:1B ladder rung, and catastrophe:general adds nuclear/natural-pandemic risk mostly unaffected by AI policy. results.title: Frontier AI Biosafety Thresholds - Frontier Model Forum
results.content: Uplift studies are well-suited to showing whether an AI system is able to assist non-experts in troubleshooting protocols related to the production of bioweapons. They may also provide insight into whether an AI system can help with the acquisition of materials and equipment required for the creation of a biological threat, support the release or deployment of biological weapons, or facilitate operational execution of the attack and avoid law enforcement detection. [...] | Anthropic | CBRN-3: The ability to significantly assist individuals or groups with basic STEM backgrounds in obtaining, producing, or deploying CBRN weapons. Assessed by comparing what potential attackers could achieve with full model access versus 2023-level online resources, assuming they have funding and up to one year of time to invest, but no initial specialized expertise.  CBRN-4: The ability to substantially uplift CBRN development capabilities of moderately resourced state programs [...] Threat Actor Uplift. All current thresholds focus on frontier AI’s ability to provide assistance or “uplift” that enhances human capabilities beyond what would otherwise be possible, bridging the expertise gap between individuals or groups with limited scientific training and those with specialized knowledge necessary for creating biological threats.

label: Fable 5
rationale: Base rates first: cumulative AI-related cyber/fraud damages already run $1-2B+/year (Surfshark $1.65B deepfake losses in 2025; FBI IC3 ~$0.9B AI-assisted losses; IBM 2026: 25% of breaches AI-enabled), so the lowest AI/cyber rungs ($1B, then $10B) are near-certain within short horizons, while no AI-related engineered epidemic or $1B misalignment incident has yet occurred, keeping those ladders 1-2 orders of magnitude lower near-term. Severity rungs decay by roughly 2-4x per 10x threshold for cyber (heavy-tailed but capped: killing 10k+ via cyber is hard), and by only ~1.5-2x per rung for bio at long horizons (engineered pandemics have fat severity tails; frontier models are near CBRN uplift thresholds per Anthropic's Aug 2026 risk report). Long-horizon top-tier numbers anchor on XPT superforecaster medians (~1% AI extinction-scale, ~5-10% any 10% catastrophe by 2100) adjusted modestly upward for faster-than-expected capability gains; catastrophe:ai 2050/2100 is set consistent with the ai:1B ladder rung, and catastrophe:general adds nuclear/natural-pandemic risk mostly unaffected by AI policy. Policy conditions: sq slightly raises long-run risk vs unconditional (unconditional embeds some chance of future stringent regulation); P1 preemption slightly raises risk; effects scale with severity and horizon—P2a/P3a/P4 (US-only) cut mid/large-tail risks ~10-20% (China and open-weights channels unaffected), P2b/P3b (US+China binding) cut them ~25-35%, and P5 (bundle) cuts large tails ~45-55%; all policies have minimal effect on the near-term low rungs, which are driven by already-deployed models and criminal adoption. Disempowerment probabilities reflect gradual-loss-of-control pathways dominating by 2100; liability (P4) helps least there since diffuse disempowerment is not readily compensable harm.
key_sources: IBM 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report (25% of breaches AI-enabled, $6M avg)
Surfshark 2026 deepfake fraud loss tracking ($2.19B cumulative, $1.65B in 2025)
FBI IC3 2025 Annual Report (~$893M AI-assisted crime losses)
Anthropic August 2026 Risk Report (models near CB-2/CBRN thresholds)
XPT (Forecasting Research Institute) superforecaster vs expert catastrophic risk estimates

label: Gemini 3.1 Pro
rationale: I estimated base rates for catastrophic risks by considering historical precedents, the current trajectory of AI capabilities, and the specific definitions of each severity threshold. For short-term horizons (6mo, 12mo), the probability of extreme events (e.g., >1M deaths) is vanishingly small, driven primarily by the time required to develop, deploy, and scale such capabilities or pathogens. As the horizon extends to 2050 and 2100, the cumulative probability increases significantly, reflecting the likelihood of transformative AI development. Cyber incidents are the most likely vector for lower-severity economic damages, while engineered pandemics (bio) dominate the higher-severity mortality risks. Misaligned AI incidents become a major factor in the long term. To evaluate the policy conditions, I applied a consistent set of multipliers to the status quo (sq) baseline. Federal preemption (P1) slightly increases risk (1.05x) by removing state-level safeguards without guaranteeing strong federal alternatives. Compute caps (P2a, P2b) reduce risk, with a bilateral US-China agreement (P2b) having a much stronger effect (0.75x) than a unilateral US policy (0.90x). Pre-release authorization (P3a, P3b) similarly reduces risk, especially if implemented internationally (0.70x). Strict liability (P4) creates strong financial incentives for safety, reducing risk by 0.80x. The bundled policy (P5) combines the most effective measures, leading to a dramatic reduction in catastrophic risk (0.50x). The unconditional forecast assumes a 0.95x multiplier, reflecting a modest probability that some beneficial policies will be implemented even without the specific conditions.
key_sources: Our World in Data: Historical pandemic and mortality base rates
Metaculus: AI timeline and catastrophic risk consensus forecasts
Epoch AI: Compute trends and frontier model projections

rationale: I estimated base rates for catastrophic risks by considering historical precedents, the current trajectory of AI capabilities, and the specific definitions of each severity threshold. For short-term horizons (6mo, 12mo), the probability of extreme events (e.g., >1M deaths) is vanishingly small, driven primarily by the time required to develop, deploy, and scale such capabilities or pathogens. As the horizon extends to 2050 and 2100, the cumulative probability increases significantly, reflecting the likelihood of transformative AI development. Cyber incidents are the most likely vector for lower-severity economic damages, while engineered pandemics (bio) dominate the higher-severity mortality risks. Misaligned AI incidents become a major factor in the long term. To evaluate the policy conditions, I applied a consistent set of multipliers to the status quo (sq) baseline. Federal preemption (P1) slightly increases risk (1.05x) by removing state-level safeguards without guaranteeing strong federal alternatives. Compute caps (P2a, P2b) reduce risk, with a bilateral US-China agreement (P2b) having a much stronger effect (0.75x) than a unilateral US policy (0.90x). Pre-release authorization (P3a, P3b) similarly reduces risk, especially if implemented internationally (0.70x). Strict liability (P4) creates strong financial incentives for safety, reducing risk by 0.80x. The bundled policy (P5) combines the most effective measures, leading to a dramatic reduction in catastrophic risk (0.50x). The unconditional forecast assumes a 0.95x multiplier, reflecting a modest probability that some beneficial policies will be implemented even without the specific conditions.

For short-term horizons (6mo, 12mo), the probability of extreme events (e.g., >1M deaths) is vanishingly small, driven primarily by the time required to develop, deploy, and scale such capabilities or pathogens. As the horizon extends to 2050 and 2100, the cumulative probability increases significantly, reflecting the likelihood of transformative AI development. Cyber incidents are the most likely vector for lower-severity economic damages, while engineered pandemics (bio) dominate the higher-severity mortality risks. Misaligned AI incidents become a major factor in the long term. To evaluate the policy conditions, I applied a consistent set of multipliers to the status quo (sq) baseline. Federal preemption (P1) slightly increases risk (1.05x) by removing state-level safeguards without guaranteeing strong federal alternatives. Compute caps (P2a, P2b) reduce risk, with a bilateral US-China agreement (P2b) having a much stronger effect (0.75x) than a unilateral US policy (0.90x). Pre-release authorization (P3a, P3b) similarly reduces risk, especially if implemented internationally (0.70x). Strict liability (P4) creates strong financial incentives for safety, reducing risk by 0.80x. The bundled policy (P5) combines the most effective measures, leading to a dramatic reduction in catastrophic risk (0.50x). The unconditional forecast assumes a 0.95x multiplier, reflecting a modest probability that some beneficial policies will be implemented even without the specific conditions.

rationale: I estimated base rates for catastrophic risks by considering historical precedents, the current trajectory of AI capabilities, and the specific definitions of each severity threshold. For short-term horizons (6mo, 12mo), the probability of extreme events (e.g., >1M deaths) is vanishingly small, driven primarily by the time required to develop, deploy, and scale such capabilities or pathogens. As the horizon extends to 2050 and 2100, the cumulative probability increases significantly, reflecting the likelihood of transformative AI development. Cyber incidents are the most likely vector for lower-severity economic damages, while engineered pandemics (bio) dominate the higher-severity mortality risks. Misaligned AI incidents become a major factor in the long term. To evaluate the policy conditions, I applied a consistent set of multipliers to the status quo (sq) baseline. Federal preemption (P1) slightly increases risk (1.05x) by removing state-level safeguards without guaranteeing strong federal alternatives. Compute caps (P2a, P2b) reduce risk, with a bilateral US-China agreement (P2b) having a much stronger effect (0.75x) than a unilateral US policy (0.90x). Pre-release authorization (P3a, P3b) similarly reduces risk, especially if implemented internationally (0.70x). Strict liability (P4) creates strong financial incentives for safety, reducing risk by 0.80x. The bundled policy (P5) combines the most effective measures, leading to a dramatic reduction in catastrophic risk (0.50x). The unconditional forecast assumes a 0.95x multiplier, reflecting a modest probability that some beneficial policies will be implemented even without the specific conditions.

rationale: I estimated base rates for catastrophic risks by considering historical precedents, the current trajectory of AI capabilities, and the specific definitions of each severity threshold. For short-term horizons (6mo, 12mo), the probability of extreme events (e.g., >1M deaths) is vanishingly small, driven primarily by the time required to develop, deploy, and scale such capabilities or pathogens. As the horizon extends to 2050 and 2100, the cumulative probability increases significantly, reflecting the likelihood of transformative AI development. Cyber incidents are the most likely vector for lower-severity economic damages, while engineered pandemics (bio) dominate the higher-severity mortality risks. Misaligned AI incidents become a major factor in the long term. To evaluate the policy conditions, I applied a consistent set of multipliers to the status quo (sq) baseline. Federal preemption (P1) slightly increases risk (1.05x) by removing state-level safeguards without guaranteeing strong federal alternatives. Compute caps (P2a, P2b) reduce risk, with a bilateral US-China agreement (P2b) having a much stronger effect (0.75x) than a unilateral US policy (0.90x). Pre-release authorization (P3a, P3b) similarly reduces risk, especially if implemented internationally (0.70x). Strict liability (P4) creates strong financial incentives for safety, reducing risk by 0.80x. The bundled policy (P5) combines the most effective measures, leading to a dramatic reduction in catastrophic risk (0.50x). The unconditional forecast assumes a 0.95x multiplier, reflecting a modest probability that some beneficial policies will be implemented even without the specific conditions.

label: Gemini 3.1 Pro
rationale: I estimated base rates for catastrophic risks by considering historical precedents, the current trajectory of AI capabilities, and the specific definitions of each severity threshold. For short-term horizons (6mo, 12mo), the probability of extreme events (e.g., >1M deaths) is vanishingly small, driven primarily by the time required to develop, deploy, and scale such capabilities or pathogens. As the horizon extends to 2050 and 2100, the cumulative probability increases significantly, reflecting the likelihood of transformative AI development. Cyber incidents are the most likely vector for lower-severity economic damages, while engineered pandemics (bio) dominate the higher-severity mortality risks. Misaligned AI incidents become a major factor in the long term. To evaluate the policy conditions, I applied a consistent set of multipliers to the status quo (sq) baseline. Federal preemption (P1) slightly increases risk (1.05x) by removing state-level safeguards without guaranteeing strong federal alternatives. Compute caps (P2a, P2b) reduce risk, with a bilateral US-China agreement (P2b) having a much stronger effect (0.75x) than a unilateral US policy (0.90x). Pre-release authorization (P3a, P3b) similarly reduces risk, especially if implemented internationally (0.70x). Strict liability (P4) creates strong financial incentives for safety, reducing risk by 0.80x. The bundled policy (P5) combines the most effective measures, leading to a dramatic reduction in catastrophic risk (0.50x). The unconditional forecast assumes a 0.95x multiplier, reflecting a modest probability that some beneficial policies will be implemented even without the specific conditions.
